d: One command installs the fleetd CLI, plus the desktop app on a machine with a display.
x: curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh In a terminal it then starts the setup wizard, fleetd init : see Quick start . Without a terminal, or with --no-init , it only installs and prints the next command. Platforms CLI (hub and workers) Desktop app Linux x64 yes yes macOS, Apple silicon yes yes macOS, Intel yes yes The hub also needs git , and the claude and gh CLIs logged in to your own accounts. A worker needs only claude . fleetd init checks each one and prints the install command for anything missing. What it installs The CLI at ~/.fleetd/bin/fleetd , linked from ~/.local/bin/fleetd . The desktop app, on macOS and on Linux with a display: ~/Applications/fleetd.app , or ~/.local/share/fleetd/app with a menu entry. Every download is checked against the release's SHA256SUMS . The installer needs no sudo, and only fleetd init sets up services. Running it again replaces what it installed. To read it first, open fleetd.sh/install.sh . Options curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh -s -- --app # the app too, on Linux without a display curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh -s -- --no-app # the CLI only curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh -s -- --no-init # install, don't start the wizard Without a terminal (here, a script): curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh -s -- --app Releases are nightly builds for now. FLEETD_CHANNEL=stable picks the stable channel once it has a release. Verify fleetd version If your shell can't find fleetd , add ~/.local/bin to your PATH , or run ~/.local/bin/fleetd .

d: One command installs and sets up fleetd; then send your first order.
x: fleetd runs Claude Code on your machines: you type what you want, and it plans the work, runs the agents, opens pull requests it has checked, and asks you only about real decisions. You need: macOS or Linux x64, the claude CLI logged in (fleetd uses your own claude setup, including any proxy in ~/.claude/settings.json ), git , and gh for pull requests. About a minute later the hub runs on this machine, the app is paired, and you type your first order. 1. Install and set up On the always-on machine that will be your hub: curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh It installs fleetd and starts the setup wizard, fleetd init . Enter takes the default at each question, and a ✗ line ends with the command that fixes it. Run fleetd init again at any time: it keeps what works and repairs the rest. curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh -s -- --no-init only installs. curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh The hub listens on your tailnet when the wizard finds Tailscale; you can also pick this machine only or your LAN. It never opens the hub to the internet. 2. Send your first order On the hub machine, if it has a desktop, the app is installed too and pairs by itself when you open it. To work from another computer, install fleetd there without the wizard and open the app: curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh -s -- --no-init open ~/Applications/fleetd.app # macOS ~/.local/share/fleetd/app/fleetd-app & # Linux (or "fleetd" in your app menu) Enter the hub address and the pairing code fleetd init printed. Codes last 15 minutes; fleetd pair on the hub prints a new one. The app opens on the board, ready to type: enter an order, such as fix the typo in the README , and press Enter. The order starts the project's lead, which answers with a brief and starts work. Its questions land in the inbox (⌘I, Ctrl+I on Linux). Next: Concepts , or more machines .

d: The hub, nodes, leads, orders, asks and the merge train, one short section each.
x: Hub One per fleet, on an always-on machine ( fleetd hub start , run as a service by fleetd init ). It holds everything that lasts: projects, leads, briefs, tasks, asks and decisions, the merge train, checks and wakes. It serves the desktop app and one MCP endpoint, <hub url>/mcp , over all your machines. Its data is one SQLite file in ~/.fleetd/hub . Nodes One fleetd node per machine that runs agents (a worker). The node dials out to the hub, so no worker opens a port. It runs one claude process per live session, each writer in its own git worktree and branch. Sessions use your own claude setup in ~/.claude : the same login, proxy settings and MCP servers as the claude in your shell. The hub machine is usually a worker too. Leads Each project has one lead: a long-running claude session that turns orders into briefs, splits them into tasks for writer and reviewer sessions, and never writes code itself. Leads run on claude-opus-5-5 by default. A project's first order starts its lead. Orders An order is one line of intent, such as fix the typo in the README , sent from the app or with intake_submit over MCP. The hub picks the project (a leading @project names it), opens a workstream and wakes the lead. The lead freezes a brief with done-when checks, then spawns tasks. A slot board caps how many sessions run at once. Asks and decisions A lead asks you only about product calls, money, credentials and irreversible steps. Asks arrive numbered, in batches, in the app's inbox; you answer tersely ( 1 go 2 nvm 3 b ). Each answer becomes a decision in a searchable log, and an ask that a past decision already answers comes back at once without bothering you. Some asks need more than words: approving an exact command, ticking off steps, or entering a secret. See Approvals & secrets . Merge train Only fleetd merges. Each writer's PR goes on its repo's train, one serial queue per repo. The train rebases each ready change onto its base, waits for CI on that exact head and squash-merges it. A change's tier sets its reviews: S needs none, M one clean review, L two plus a verifier, each bound to the current patch. A PR body needs a Source: line naming what it serves. You can freeze a repo's train with train_freeze . Done, checked A lead can't just say "done". fleetd claim done makes the hub run the workstream's done-when checks itself (a PR merged, CI green, a command or test on a machine, an HTTP check, a judge, a person), and only all of them passing makes it done. Each claim keeps its evidence and exit codes.

d: Add workers to the hub, log in their Claude, remove them, and check their health.
h: Add a machine the hub can reach over SSH
Add a machine the hub can't reach
x: A worker is any machine that runs agents. It needs the claude CLI, and for now the same OS and CPU as the hub. Run these on the hub. Add a machine the hub can reach over SSH Run fleetd init again and pick it from the list (hosts from ~/.ssh/config and your tailnet), or name it: fleetd machine add homeserver It copies the hub's own fleetd there, enrolls the node with a one-time token, runs it as a user service and waits until the machine is online. It prints every remote command before it runs it. --dry-run only prints the plan: fleetd machine add builder-1 --dry-run It is safe to run again: a real run reads the machine's state first and skips what is done. Add this machine fleetd machine add --local The same steps, run here without SSH. Use it to make the hub machine a worker too, or to repair it. fleetd init does this when you pick "(this machine)". Add a machine the hub can't reach For a laptop behind NAT, or anything without SSH from the hub, print a one-line join command on the hub and paste it on the new machine: fleetd pair --worker laptop The code lasts 15 minutes. The machine must reach the hub's address. Run the command again later to repair the worker; --rejoin enrolls it again with a new code. Claude on a worker Sessions use the worker's own claude setup ( ~/.claude ), so if claude works in your shell there, it works for fleetd: your login, a proxy set in ~/.claude/settings.json and your MCP servers included. If it is not logged in, log in as you normally do: claude auth login Behind a proxy, log in with your proxy instead. fleetd doctor shows each worker's claude, login and proxy. See The Claude login for a dedicated profile per machine. Remove a machine fleetd machine remove homeserver It stops and removes the node's service there and revokes its key on the hub. --purge also deletes ~/.fleetd/node and ~/.fleetd/claude.env on that machine; your own ~/.claude stays. For a machine that joined with pair --worker , only the key is revoked; stop its node there yourself: fleetd machine remove laptop Check health fleetd doctor It checks the hub and every machine (online, claude version and login, commit identity, disk, usage breaker) and prints the fix for each problem. The app's Machines screen shows the same checks. Every finding and its fix: Troubleshooting .

d: Add a project, send an order, follow it, and see how "done" is checked.
h: Add to it, steer it, stop it
x: Add a project Run fleetd init again and pick a repo: a checkout it finds on a worker, or a GitHub URL, which it clones. The rest of your setup stays as it is. From an MCP client, project_add {machineId, path, title} adds one and project_remove {machineId, projectId} forgets it (its files, branches and worktrees stay). Its lead Each project has one lead, and the project's first order starts it: there is nothing to start by hand. The lead's first message lists the order, and the app shows the lead starting. If the lead can't start, because claude on the worker is logged out or outside the supported version range, or the worker is offline, the order waits. The app's reply says why and what to run on the worker. Once the worker comes back online with a usable claude , its lead starts and picks up every waiting order. To choose the lead's model and effort, or to start it before any order, call lead_start {machineId, projectId, model, effort} from an MCP client; the model and effort are saved for the project (default claude-opus-5-5 , high). To keep a project's lead from starting by itself, set lead.autoStart: false in its policy file : orders then wait until lead_start , and the reply says so. Connect an MCP client The hub's MCP endpoint is <hub url>/mcp . Give the client an agent key, shown once: fleetd hub key create --name ci-bot --role operate --machines '*' For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http fleetd http://hub.your-tailnet.ts.net:4790/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer fld_<key>" Roles are read , operate and admin , on every machine ( '*' ) or a list. fleetd hub key list shows keys and fleetd hub key revoke <keyId> ends one at once. Send an order In the app, type one line in the board's composer and press Enter ( Give work ). Pick the project, or leave it to the hub, which reads a leading @project , else asks a quick router, else asks you. A prefix picks the playbook: fix: or bug: , research: , finish: . Attach screenshots or files, or @ -mention files, orders and PRs; the lead gets them with the order. From an MCP client: intake_submit {text} ; intake_preview {text} says where it would go without sending it. Follow it The lead freezes a brief, runs writer and reviewer tasks on your workers, and puts each PR on the merge train. The board shows every order's phase and live agents; open one for its PRs, checks and the lead's conversation ( Follow an order ). Add to it, steer it, stop it In the order, Enter adds a note the lead reads at its next wake; ⌘Enter (Ctrl+Enter) or "Steer now" wakes it now. Stop cancels the order's running and queued agents and withdraws its asks; merged PRs stay. A stopped order stays stopped: send it again as a new order. Answer its questions Questions land in the inbox (⌘I), numbered. Reply in one line, such as 1 go 2 nvm 3 b : see the reply grammar . Commands and secrets have their own flow: Approvals & secrets . Done, checked The lead reports done with fleetd claim done . The hub then runs the brief's done-when checks itself, and only all of them passing makes the workstream done. A failure wakes the lead with the exit code and output. claims_list shows every claim with its evidence. A done order cleans up after itself: its PRs that aren't merged and aren't on the train (queued, reviewing, ready, rebasing, CI failed) are closed with a comment saying why, and its leftover tasks are cancelled. A PR the train is already landing is left to land. MCP tools for orders Tool Does Role intake_submit {text} send an order (optional attachments , refs ) operate intake_preview {text} where it would go, without sending operate attachment_put {name, mime, dataB64} upload a file (image, text or PDF, at most 5 MiB) for an order or note operate project_files {machineId, projectId, query} a project's files for @ -mentions read orders_board {projectRef?} open orders with their phase, agents, PRs, asks and the trains read order_get {workstreamId} one order, plus its lead, finished agents and claims read order_note {workstreamId, text, urgent?} add to an order; urgent wakes the lead now operate, human key order_stop {workstreamId} stop an order operate, human key workstream_list , workstream_get , thread_tail , fleetd_status the lower-level views read events_wait long-polls for changes instead of polling. A human key is a person's paired device, not an agent key.

d: The asks only a person answers, from the desktop app: commands, tool prompts, checklists and secrets.
x: These asks come to the inbox like any other, but only a person's device answers them (a human key, which the app holds). An agent key can't, and "recs fine" or "all go" never answers them in bulk. Approve a command When a lead needs an irreversible, money or credential step, it files the exact command with fleetd gated run . You see the command, the reason and where it runs. Reply <n> go to run it or <n> no to refuse. The node runs exactly the stored bytes, in the project's workspace, and the exit code and output go back to the lead. Tool permission prompts Leads and tasks run with claude's permission prompts off. A session started with thread_launch and runtimeMode: approval-required sends each prompt to you as an approve ask instead. A prompt that stays open is raised again after 10 minutes, then every 30. A project can answer prompts itself with rules in claude's own syntax in .fleetd/policy.yaml : tools: allow: ["Bash(npm test:*)", "Read"] deny: ["Bash(git push:*)"] A deny rule wins over an allow rule. Rules apply to every session in the project; see Config & files . Checklists Some steps only you can do, such as clicking through a provider's console. The lead files them as a checklist ask ( fleetd ask --kind do ). Reply <n> done once you've done them. If the ask has a check, the hub runs it, and a failure reopens the ask with the evidence. Secrets When a lead needs an API key or password, it files a secret ask that names the machine and where the value goes (an env file line or a file). Type the value in the app. The app seals it to that machine's key (a libsodium sealed box) and wipes what you typed. The hub relays the ciphertext without storing it, the node writes it (mode 0600), and the lead only ever sees its fingerprint. The target machine must be online: nothing is queued. A gated command can use a stored secret as an environment variable ( --secret-env ); the node reads it from its own files.

d: Every prompt fleetd sends a model, how to read, edit, reset and diff it, your own instructions, and what a running agent keeps.
h: How a session gets its instructions
When fleetd changes a default you edited
See exactly what an agent was told
Not editable: tool descriptions and CLI replies
x: Every word fleetd sends a model is listed here, readable in the app and the CLI, and editable. A session keeps the text it started with. How a session gets its instructions There is no hidden system prompt. fleetd's instructions are the first message of a session (lead, task, reviewer, judge), later messages into it (wakes, review findings, train news, nudges), or the input of a one-shot claude -p with no tools (the router, the retro). Your own claude setup applies as usual underneath ( Config & files ). The prompts Grouped as in Settings → Prompts. Group Ids Sent Lead lead.start , lead.digest at lead start and every restart; the digest also tops every wake Tasks task.brief.write , task.brief.read , task.brief.review , task.review_findings , task.train_rebase , task.train_ci_failed at each task attempt, then into it Reviews and checks review.reviewer , review.verifier , judge , judge.research per PR head by review tier; per judge done-when check Wakes and messages wake.* , digest.* , watchdog.nudge , usage.continue , permission.denied.* into a running session: one line per event, a stalled run, a usage reset, a refused tool call One-shots router , router.retry , retro per order without a project; per retro run Playbooks playbook.feature , playbook.bugfix , playbook.research , playbook.finish-all in the lead's digest while an order uses it fleetd prompts list prints them all with where each comes from; fleetd prompts show <id> prints one. Safety rules: code or prompt Most rules don't depend on the prompt. fleetd enforces them in code whatever the text says: secrets are sealed to a machine, gated commands wait for your tap, only the train merges, and done is decided by the hub running the checks. Editing those words away only means agents hit refusals they weren't warned about. A few rules live only in the prompt: reviewers don't read the PR description, no subagents, the lead never writes code, a lead doesn't re-ask a decided question, and it asks you only about product, money, credentials or something irreversible. Remove one of these and nothing else stops it. Edit a prompt In the app: Settings → Prompts. Pick Global or a project at the top, open a prompt, edit, Save. Reset to default and Diff are next to Save. On the hub machine: fleetd prompts edit lead.start fleetd prompts edit task.brief.write --project builder-1/app fleetd prompts diff lead.start fleetd prompts reset lead.start edit opens $VISUAL or $EDITOR , shows the warnings and asks before saving. A project's version beats the global one, which beats fleetd's. Playbooks have only the global level. Your versions are files under ~/.fleetd/hub/prompts/ ( Config & files ); edit them with fleetd prompts edit , not by hand. Prompts fill in {{name}} placeholders, such as {{project}} ; the editor lists each prompt's own. Nothing else is template syntax. Warnings Saving never refuses text that isn't empty, but it warns: Warning Means a required placeholder is missing that value no longer reaches the agent (for task.brief.write without {{serves}} , the PR's Source: line) unknown placeholder {{name}} isn't one this prompt fills; it is sent as written a safety rule is missing its wording is gone; the warning says whether fleetd still enforces it in code or nothing does too long past the prompt's budget; the digest cuts long playbook lines Your own instructions Settings → Instructions, Global or per project, or: fleetd instructions edit fleetd instructions edit --project builder-1/app They are added to every lead's first message and every task brief (writers, reviewers and judges), global first, under "Custom instructions from the human". Not to the router, the retro or wakes. When fleetd changes a default you edited Your version stays in use. The prompt gets an "update" chip in Settings → Prompts; fleetd prompts diff <id> shows what changed in fleetd's text and in yours since you edited it, and edit opens a merge of both. Save it, keep yours, or reset. A safety rule the new default added and your text lacks shows as a warning. Playbooks are the exception: an edited playbook gets no notice when fleetd's version changes. Compare it yourself with fleetd prompts diff playbook.<name> after an update. What a running agent keeps Each session keeps the exact prompt versions it started with, wakes included. An edit reaches new sessions at once: a task at its next attempt, a lead at its next start. To give a running lead your edit now, restart it with lead_restart from an MCP client ( Its lead ). See exactly what an agent was told In an order, a lane's menu or the lead's header has "Show full prompt": the exact first message, which versions it used (default, edited globally, project), your instructions, and the tools it may not use. Or: fleetd prompts show --session <machine>/<thread> Later messages are in the lead's conversation. Not editable: tool descriptions and CLI replies MCP tool descriptions and what the lead-side CLI prints back (each next: and fix: ) are the other half of a protocol with code: a description must match its tool, a next: must name a real command. They are listed in the CLI reference and the MCP tools , not editable.

d: Pair the app with your hub, give the fleet work from the board, follow an order, answer the inbox, and the shortcuts.
x: The app is where you give work, follow it, answer asks, approve commands and enter secrets. Install it with curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh -s -- --app ( Install ). Pair it with the hub On the hub machine the app pairs by itself. On another computer, print a code on the hub: fleetd pair Enter the address and code on the app's "Connect to your fleetd hub" screen, or open the fleetd://pair link. The code works once, for 15 minutes. The app keeps its key in the OS keychain, never in a file. Settings (⌘,) shows the hub it is paired with and disconnects it; "Connect to a hub…" in the palette pairs with another. The board The app opens on the board with the composer focused: type what the fleet should do and press Enter. Under it, what needs you, then every open order grouped by project (⌘⇧G groups by status). Each card shows its phase, up to four live agents (role, what each is doing now), its PRs and the lead's next step. Cards don't move under the pointer or the selection; they resort 2 s after you leave. Machine load and the merge train sit in strips at the bottom. The sidebar lists Board, Machines, and each project with its orders; an amber dot means an order needs you. Hold ⌘ to see the ⌘1-⌘9 jump keys. Give work Project : the picker (⌘⇧P) says where the order goes and why: chosen, selected in the sidebar, the router's guess, last used, or "the hub picks". A leading @project also picks it. Type : the type picker (⌘⇧T), or a prefix: fix: or bug: , research: , finish: . The default is a feature. Attach : up to 8 files (images, text, PDF; 5 MiB each) by "+ attach" (⌘⇧A), paste or drop. A paste over 3,500 bytes becomes pasted-N.txt . The lead finds them in .fleetd/attachments/<W>/ of the project, kept out of git. Mention : @ opens a menu of the project's files, orders and PRs; ↑ ↓ and Enter or Tab pick one. An order is at most 4,000 bytes; attach the detail. It appears as a card at once. If the hub can't tell the project, the card asks which one; if sending fails, it offers Retry and Edit. In an order, ⌘N opens a composer over it, so you keep your place. Follow an order Click a card (or select it and press Enter). The left side has its agents, PRs and done-when checks with their results; the right side is the project lead's conversation, focused on this order: finished turns fold to one line ("Worked for 48s · ran 3 commands") and runs about other orders collapse. The box under the conversation talks to the lead: Do How The lead Add a note Enter reads it at its next wake Steer ⌘Enter, or "Steer now" is woken now Stop "Stop W…" (⌘.), then confirm its running agents are cancelled and its asks withdrawn; merged PRs stay Reorder "Reorder" on a stopped order nothing yet: its text goes back into the composer, to send as a new order A stopped order isn't reopened. ⌘ [ and ⌘ ] go to the previous and next order, Esc back to the board. Inbox and replies ⌘I opens the inbox panel; the badge in the title bar counts what needs you. In the panel, 1-9 select an item, Enter takes its recommendation, n answers no, Esc closes. Or answer a whole batch in one line in its reply field: Reply Means 1 go accept item 1 (also yes , y , ok , rec ) 2 nvm reject item 2 (also no , drop , skip , n ) 3 b pick option b of item 3 ( a to f ) 1-3 go the same answer for items 1 to 3 2: use the staging bucket answer in your own words 4 later not now; it stays open 5 done you did a checklist's steps recs fine accept every recommendation not mentioned #B4 1 go answer batch 4, not the latest pref: no new dependencies a standing preference for every lead forget D12 drop decision 12 Mix them: 1 go 2 nvm 3 b . A reply the app can't read changes nothing and shows a hint. Asks that block work also raise a desktop notification: at most one every 20 minutes, with the rest folded in as "+N more", and only urgent ones in quiet hours (23:00 to 08:00 unless a policy.quiet_hours decision says otherwise). Clicking it opens the ask. Settings Settings (⌘,) has Appearance, Motion and the hub connection. Motion: System follows the OS's reduce-motion setting, Reduced turns the brief card and lane transitions off, Full keeps them. Nothing in the app animates continuously. Shortcuts ⌘ on macOS is Ctrl on Linux. Keys Does ⌘N New order (over the order view when one is open) ⌘L Focus the composer ⌘K Command palette: projects, orders (by id too), asks and actions; always offers "New order: " ⌘I Inbox panel ⌘0 Board ⌘1 to ⌘9 Open the nth order in the sidebar ⌘⇧G Group the board by project or by status ⌘ [ / ⌘ ] Previous / next order ⌘. Stop the open order (asks to confirm) ⌘, Settings ⌘B Toggle the sidebar Enter Send an order; in an order, add a note ⌘Enter In an order, steer: wake the lead now Shift+Enter New line ⌘⇧P / ⌘⇧T / ⌘⇧A In the composer: project picker / type picker / attach ↑ ↓ (or j k) Move the selection on the board, in a menu or the palette (also Ctrl+P / Ctrl+N in the palette) Enter Open the selected card, run the palette item, pick from a menu Esc Close a menu, the stop confirm or the inbox panel; from an order, back to the board Tab / Shift+Tab Next / previous control ⌘Q Quit ⌃⌘F (macOS), F11 (Linux) Full screen ⌘H, ⌥⌘H, ⌘M (macOS) Hide, hide others, minimize Typing with no field focused goes to the composer on screen. Text fields follow the usual editing keys of each platform (word motion, undo and redo, select all).

d: Every fleetd command and option, generated from the binary's own help.
x:
Generated from fleetd help , so it matches the binary this site was built with. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 failed (a check that did not pass), 2 usage, 3 refused, 4 hub or node unreachable, 78 ( listen ) the hub refused the key. fleetd version print the fleetd version and protocol fleetd help show this message fleetd update [--check] [--channel ] replace this fleetd with the latest release fleetd init [--yes] [--home ] [--listen ] [--url ] [--git-identity "Name "] [--no-service] [--unit-suffix ] set up fleetd step by step in a terminal: the hub on this machine (home default ~/.fleetd/hub, kept running by a systemd or launchd user service), where it listens (your tailnet when there is one), the claude and gh logins, the machines that run agents, a first project and the desktop app, then fleetd doctor. Run it again to check and repair; it keeps what works. --yes takes every default. Without a terminal and without --yes it only sets up the hub. --url is how devices reach the hub (default http://); --git-identity is the commit author for every machine (the GitHub noreply address for public repos); --no-service prepares everything but leaves starting the hub to you fleetd init --join --code [--machine-id ] [--git-identity "Name "] [--rejoin] [--claude-config-dir ] make this machine a worker of that hub, without SSH from the hub: the command fleetd pair --worker prints on the hub. Run again, it keeps the node's enrolment and repairs the rest; --rejoin enrols again with a new code fleetd doctor [--home ] run every setup check on the hub now and print each problem with its fix fleetd uninstall [--home ] [--purge] stop and remove the hub's service; its data stays unless --purge, which also removes what an older fleetd installed for T3 Code fleetd machine add | --local [--machine-id ] [--tags a,b] [--dry-run] [--no-service] [--hub-url ] [--ssh-config ] [--home ] [--unit-suffix ] [--claude-config-dir ] set up a machine that runs agents, over SSH (--local: this machine): copies this fleetd there, checks its claude (installed, version >=2.1.300, <2.2.0, logged in), enrolls the node and runs it as a user service, then waits until the machine is online; prints every command first, --dry-run only prints (for a fresh machine, without connecting); --no-service enrolls the node but writes no service and prints how to run it; safe to run again fleetd machine remove [--purge] [--home ] stop and remove the node's service on the machine and revoke its key on the hub; --purge also deletes ~/.fleetd/node and ~/.fleetd/claude.env there, and what an older fleetd installed for T3 Code fleetd pair [--name ] [--home ] print a one-time code (15 min) that pairs the desktop app with this hub; the app on this machine pairs by itself fleetd pair --worker [--home ] print the one command that makes another machine a worker of this hub, with a one-time code (15 min): for a machine the hub can't reach over SSH fleetd hub start [--home ] [--listen ] [--queue-ttl ] [--router-model ] run the hub (default home ~/.fleetd/hub, listen 127.0.0.1:4790, writes to an offline machine wait 24 h, intents without a project are routed by the claude CLI with claude-haiku-5-5) fleetd hub key create --name --role --machines <'*'|id,id> [--home ] create an agent key for the MCP endpoint; d: Where fleetd keeps its state, the Claude login it uses, the project policy file, and its port.
x: ~/.fleetd Prompts and instructions: What agents are told . fleetd uninstall keeps all of it; see Updating & uninstall . The Claude login Sessions run claude with your own setup on that machine ( ~/.claude ), so your login, the env in ~/.claude/settings.json (a proxy's ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL , say), an apiKeyHelper and your MCP servers work as they do in your shell. If claude works for you on the worker, it works for fleetd. Otherwise log in as you normally do: claude auth login , or through your proxy. fleetd doctor shows what each worker uses, e.g. claude 2.1.302, logged in (Max), via proxy http://127.0.0.1:8317 from ~/.claude/settings.json . fleetd adds its own settings per session on top of yours, never in their place: an --mcp-config for its servers and a --settings overlay that pins claude's version and denies the tools agents never get (subagents, plan mode, worktrees, cron). To give a worker's sessions a dedicated claude profile instead, set "claudeConfigDir": "<dir>" in ~/.fleetd/node/node.json (or join with fleetd node join --claude-config-dir <dir> ) and restart the node. A session resumes only under the config dir it started in; the node refuses a resume under another one and says so. The hub's own claude (the order router and the retro) uses your normal login on the hub machine ( ~/.claude ), or the gateway variables in claude.env . claude.env Optional. KEY=VALUE lines for the claude that fleetd runs, for a variable your login needs that the services don't see, such as one only your interactive shell exports. Blank lines, # comments and export are allowed. Mode 0600. Your ~/.claude/settings.json env outranks it, as it does for your own claude . CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=<token from claude setup-token> # or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://gateway.example.com ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=<token> Nodes add every line to each session's environment and re-read the file at each start. The hub service loads the file when it starts, so restart it after a change. Its own claude gets only ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL , ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from it. .fleetd/policy.yaml An optional file in a project's repo; commit it to the default branch. Changes apply within a minute. Without it, writers may touch the whole repo. areas: # what a writer task may touch; a task leases one or more areas docs: ["docs/**"] app: ["src/**", "package.json"] defaults: # optional: the project's task model and effort (low, medium, high, max) model: claude-opus-5-5 effort: high finishAll: # optional maxChildren: 10 # most child workstreams one finish-all run starts tools: # optional: claude permission rules for every session allow: ["Bash(npm test:*)"] deny: ["Bash(git push:*)"] lead: # optional autoStart: false # orders wait for lead_start instead of starting the lead (default true) Area names are lowercase slugs. A broken file is refused with the exact problem, never ignored, so a typo can't widen what a writer may touch. Services fleetd init and fleetd machine add run the hub and node as user services: Linux (systemd) macOS (launchd) Hub ~/.config/systemd/user/fleetd-hub.service ~/Library/LaunchAgents/sh.fleetd.hub.plist Node ~/.config/systemd/user/fleetd-node.service ~/Library/LaunchAgents/sh.fleetd.node.plist --unit-suffix <s> adds a suffix to these names, for a second fleet on one machine. Ports and addresses The hub listens on one port, 4790 by default: on your tailnet address when fleetd init finds Tailscale, otherwise on 127.0.0.1 only. The desktop app, nodes and MCP clients all use it ( <hub url>/mcp for MCP). Workers open no port: their nodes dial out. Change it with fleetd init --listen <host:port> --url <url> . The app The app's pairing hand-off from fleetd init or fleetd pair on the same machine is ~/.config/fleetd/app-pair.json (macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/fleetd/app-pair.json ). Its hub key is in the OS keychain.

d: What fleetd trusts, how keys and secrets move, and how to report a vulnerability.
x: fleetd is built for one person or a small team running their own fleet. Network The hub is never public by default. fleetd init listens on your tailnet address, or on 127.0.0.1 without Tailscale. Plain HTTP is accepted only there (Tailscale's tunnel is encrypted); anywhere else, put HTTPS in front ( the https check ). Nodes dial out. A worker's node connects to the hub and proves itself with its own key pair, so no worker opens a port. Enrollment tokens and pairing codes work once and expire after 15 minutes. Keys Agent keys are hashed. A fld_ key is shown once; the hub stores only its hash and prefix. Each key has read, operate or admin rights on every machine or a named list. A revoked key stops on its next request. A person's device holds a human key , in the OS keychain, never in a file. Only human keys answer secret, approve and checklist asks, so no agent can approve itself. The node socket trusts the node's OS user. Lead-side commands reach the hub through ~/.fleetd/node/node.sock (mode 0600), and the hub attributes each call to the project whose workspace contains the caller's working directory. Any process running as that user can act as any project's lead on that machine. Run agents you don't trust as a different user. Secrets and commands Secrets never reach the hub in plain text. The app seals each value to the target node's key (a libsodium sealed box) and wipes what was typed. The hub relays the ciphertext without storing it and keeps only the fingerprint the node reports. Notifications carry a one-line summary, never a secret. An approved command runs exactly as stored , and only after a person approves it. Webhooks are signed with a Standard Webhooks signature; each subscription's secret is shown once and stored encrypted. Software Installs are checksummed. The installer and fleetd update refuse any release file whose SHA-256 doesn't match the release's SHA256SUMS . fleetd machine add copies the hub's own binary to a worker over SSH. Models only through the claude CLI , with the machine user's own claude setup (their login, settings and MCP servers), so agents get the same Claude access as that user. fleetd never calls a model or usage API itself. Report a vulnerability Privately, through GitHub's security advisories for unlaboredlabs/fleetd .

x: fleetd doctor on the hub checks the hub and every machine, and prints each problem with its fix. The app's Machines screen shows the same checks. Fix commands run on the machine the finding names. Each section here is one check: a hub check hub/<name> is #hub-<name> , a machine check <machine>/<name> is #<name> . fleetd doctor ✗ is a failure; ! is a warning or a check that couldn't tell. The hub doesn't answer fleetd doctor Run fleetd init . If you run the hub yourself ( --no-service ), start it with fleetd hub start . The log is ~/.fleetd/hub/hub.log . The hub doesn't answer at its own address The hub does not answer at its own address http://…/healthz (…). Restart the hub service: systemctl --user restart fleetd-hub.service # Linux launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/sh.fleetd.hub # macOS gh is not installed or not logged in gh is not logged in on the hub; the merge train and PR checks need it. gh auth login If gh is missing, install it from cli.github.com first. claude on the hub is not logged in claude on the hub is not logged in; the intake router and the retro can't reach a model. claude auth login When the hub's claude goes through a proxy, the doctor names it; log in with your proxy as you normally do. For a gateway, API key or token instead, put ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN ) in ~/.fleetd/claude.env and restart the hub service: see claude.env . If claude is missing ("Claude Code (claude) is not on the hub's PATH"), install it first (next section). claude on the hub is missing or the wrong version Same findings and fixes as a worker's claude version , for the hub's own claude. Not installed: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash The hub isn't reachable over HTTPS The hub's address http://… is not HTTPS; keys from the desktop app and other machines would cross the network unencrypted. Plain HTTP passes on loopback and on a tailnet address ( 100.64.0.0/10 or a *.ts.net name). Elsewhere, serve the hub over HTTPS, then stop the hub and point fleetd at the new address: tailscale serve --bg 4790 fleetd init --url https://<that address> The same fix applies to "The hub has no address set up" and to an unreadable ~/.fleetd/hub/setup.json . When the HTTPS address stops answering, check where it points with tailscale serve status . A machine is offline or degraded laptop is offline (last seen …). · laptop is degraded: …. The finding's fix follows the cause. For claude logged out, out of range or missing, it is the login, update or install (see the claude findings below), and both in order when both are needed. Only a node that is down or has no claude cause gets a restart, on that machine: systemctl --user restart fleetd-node.service # Linux launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/sh.fleetd.node # macOS The log is ~/.fleetd/logs/node.log . claude is missing or the wrong version fleetd speaks claude's stream-json protocol, which isn't a stable API. It is tested with claude >=2.1.300, <2.2.0 (fixtures from 2.1.302). An older claude runs with a warning: fleetd checks its protocol at every start and refuses it only if something fleetd uses is missing. A claude past 2.2 is refused. Finding Status Fix claude is not installed on laptop; its sessions can't start. ✗ curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash claude 2.1.296 is older than fleetd is tested with (from 2.1.300); it may work, and fleetd checks its protocol at every start. ! claude update claude 2.2.0 is newer than this fleetd supports (>=2.1.300, < 2.2.0); its stream-json protocol may have changed. ✗ claude install 2.1.302, or fleetd update claude 2.1.303 is newer than 2.1.302, the version this fleetd was tested with. It is inside the supported range, so sessions run. ! claude install 2.1.302 claude --version printed "…", which fleetd can't read as a version. ✗ curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash -s 2.1.302 Sessions on that machine are refused until a ✗ is fixed. fleetd turns claude's auto-updater off for its own sessions. claude is not logged in on a worker laptop: claude 2.1.302, not logged in, so its sessions can't start. Sessions use the worker's own claude setup, so log in there as you would for yourself: claude auth login If claude goes through a proxy ( ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in ~/.claude/settings.json ; the doctor names it), log in with your proxy as you normally do. A login that expires mid-run ("claude refused its login: …") has the same fix. See the Claude login . claude doesn't answer the protocol probe claude on laptop did not answer fleetd's protocol probe as expected. Put the tested claude on that machine: claude install 2.1.302 " claude --version and the running claude disagree (… vs …): two installs on PATH?" means two claudes; reinstall with curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash and remove the other. "has not probed its claude yet" clears by itself a second after the node starts. No or the wrong commit identity No git commit identity is set on laptop. · Commits on laptop use … (from git's global config); the hub's identity is …. For a machine set up over SSH, write the hub's identity into its service again, from the hub: fleetd machine add laptop For the hub's own machine, the finding prints fleetd machine add --local . For one that joined with a code, run fleetd pair --worker laptop on the hub, then the command it prints on the machine. Without a hub identity, set one on the machine: git config --global user.email '<id>+<user>@users.noreply.github.com' . Low disk space … free under ~ on laptop; fleetd needs at least 5.0 GB. Each writer session gets its own git worktree, so a machine needs room. Free space under the path the finding names; df -h <path> shows what is left. The usage breaker is open New turns on laptop are paused by the usage breaker. The machine's Claude login hit a plan or rate limit, and new turns wait. Wait for the reset (the finding says when), or, once the login has capacity, call usage_resume for that machine from an MCP client.

d: Update fleetd and its app, pick a release channel, and remove fleetd from a machine.
x: Update fleetd update --check fleetd update It replaces the CLI, and the desktop app when the installer put it in its usual place, then restarts the hub and node services that run this binary. Every file is checked against the release's SHA256SUMS . Workers don't update themselves. Update the hub first, then each worker: run fleetd update there, or fleetd machine add <ssh-host> on the hub, which copies the hub's binary over. fleetd pins claude separately: see claude version . Channels fleetd update stays on the channel you installed from. Releases are nightly builds for now; a stable channel comes with the first release. fleetd update --channel stable curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | FLEETD_CHANNEL=stable sh Remove a machine From the hub: fleetd machine remove <id> , with --purge to delete its data too. See Machines . Uninstall the hub fleetd uninstall It stops and removes the hub's service (here there was none) and keeps its data. --purge also deletes ~/.fleetd/hub ; stop a hub you run yourself first. Remove each worker before you purge the hub. Remove the CLI and app curl -fsSL https://fleetd.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall It runs fleetd uninstall first, then removes the CLI and the app. ~/.fleetd stays.
